entries.10b4ead9de2b250240f751b722deb0055867ef16: <div sID="gen8207" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="2Chr.18" sID="2Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen8207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8208" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8209" type="x-p"/> The story of this chapter we had just as it is here related in the story of the reign of Ahab king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.41-2Kgs.22.50">1 Kings xxii.</reference> There it looks more creditable to Ahab than any thing else recorded of him that he was in league with so good a man as Jehoshaphat; here it is a great blemish in the reign of Jehoshaphat that he thus connected himself with so bad a man as Ahab. Here is, I. The alliance he contracted himself with Ahab, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. His consent to join with him in his expedition for the recovery of Ramoth-Gilead out of the hands of the Syrians, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2-2Chr.18.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. Their consulting with the prophets, false and true, before they went, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.4-2Chr.18.27">ver. 4-27</reference>. IV. The success of their expedition. Jehoshaphat hardly escaped (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.28-2Chr.18.32">ver. 28-32</reference>) and Ahab received his death's wound, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.33-2Chr.18.34">ver. 33, 34</reference>.
entries.90d382d34b1b0286f502403247889018b8960b21: <div eID="gen8209" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8208" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehoshaphat's Alliance with Ahab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen8210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab. <hi type="super">2</hi> And after <hi type="italic">certain</hi> years he went down to Ahab to Samaria. And Ahab killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, and for the people that <hi type="italic">he had</hi> with him, and persuaded him to go up <hi type="italic">with him</hi> to Ramoth-gilead. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Ahab king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Wilt thou go with me to Ramoth-gilead? And he answered him, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> as thou <hi type="italic">art,</hi> and my people as thy people; and <hi type="italic">we will be</hi> with thee in the war. <div eID="gen8210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8211" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Jehoshaphat growing greater. It was said before (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.5">ch. xvii. 5</reference>) that he had <hi type="italic">riches and honour in abundance;</hi> and here it is said again that his wealth and honour increased upon him by piety and good management. <div eID="gen8211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8212" type="x-p"/> II. Not growing wiser, else he would not have joined with Ahab, that degenerate Israelite, who had sold himself to work wickedness. What good could he get by a man that was so bad? What good could he do to a man that was so obstinately wicked—an idolater, a persecutor? With him he joined in affinity, that is, married his son Jehoram to Ahab's daughter Athaliah. <div eID="gen8212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8213" type="x-p"/> 1. This was the worst match that ever was made by any of the house of David. I wonder what Jehoshaphat could promise himself by it. (1.) Perhaps pride made the match, as it does many a one, which speeds accordingly. His religion forbade him to marry his son to a daughter of any of the heathen princes that were about him—<hi type="italic">Thou shalt not take their daughters to thy sons;</hi> and, having riches and honour in abundance, he thought it a disparagement to marry him to a subject. A king's daughter it must be, and therefore Ahab's, little considering that Jezebel was her mother. (2.) Some think he did it in policy, hoping by this expedient to unite the kingdoms in his son, Ahab perhaps flattering him with hopes that he would make him his heir, when he intended no such thing. <div eID="gen8213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8214" type="x-p"/> 2. This match drew Jehoshaphat, (1.) Into an intimate familiarity with Ahab. He paid him a visit at Samaria, and Ahab, proud of the honour which Jehoshaphat did him, gave him a very splendid entertainment, according to the splendour of those times: He <hi type="italic">killed sheep and oxen for him,</hi> plain meat, <hi type="italic">in abundance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2">v. 2</reference>. In this Jehoshaphat did not walk so closely as he should have done in the ways of his father David, who <hi type="italic">hated the congregation of evil-doers and would not sit with the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.5">Ps. xxvi. 5</reference>), nor desired to <hi type="italic">eat of their dainties,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">Ps. cxli. 4</reference>. (2.) Into a league with Ahab against the Syrians. Ahab persuaded him to join forces with him in an expedition for the recovery of Ramoth-Gilead, a city in the tribe of Gad, on the other side Jordan. Did not Ahab know that that, and all the other cities of Israel, did of right belong to Jehoshaphat, as heir of the house of David? With what face then could he ask Jehoshaphat to assist him in recovering it for himself, whose title to the crown was usurped and precarious? Yet Jehoshaphat, an easy man, yields to go with him: <hi type="italic">I am as thou art,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.3">v. 3</reference>. Some men's kindnesses are dangerous, as well as their society infectious. The feast Ahab made for Jehoshaphat was designed only to wheedle him into the expedition. The <hi type="italic">kisses of an enemy are deceitful.</hi>
entries.ae809b13a8227771a7e9ccc6e10036a4e1157b74: <div eID="gen8214" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophets Are Consulted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen8215" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And Jehoshaphat said unto the king of Israel, Enquire, I pray thee, at the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to day. <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore the king of Israel gathered together of prophets four hundred men, and said unto them, Shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear? And they said, Go up; for God will deliver <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the king's hand. <hi type="super">6</hi> But Jehoshaphat said, <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> not here a prophet of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> besides, that we might enquire of him? <hi type="super">7</hi> And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> yet one man, by whom we may enquire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but I hate him; for he never prophesied good unto me, but always evil: the same <hi type="italic">is</hi> Micaiah the son of Imla. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the king of Israel called for one <hi type="italic">of his</hi> officers, and said, Fetch quickly Micaiah the son of Imla. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah sat either of them on his throne, clothed in <hi type="italic">their</hi> robes, and they sat in a void place at the entering in of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets prophesied before them. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah had made him horns of iron, and said, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , With these thou shalt push Syria until they be consumed. <hi type="super">11</hi> And all the prophets prophesied so, saying, Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and prosper: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall deliver <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the hand of the king. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the messenger that went to call Micaiah spake to him, saying, Behold, the words of the prophets <hi type="italic">declare</hi> good to the king with one assent; let thy word therefore, I pray thee, be like one of theirs, and speak thou good. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Micaiah said, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, even what my God saith, that will I speak. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when he was come to the king, the king said unto him, Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear? And he said, Go ye up, and prosper, and they shall be delivered into your hand. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the king said to him, How many times shall I adjure thee that thou say nothing but the truth to me in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">16</hi> Then he said, I did see all Israel scattered upon the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, These have no master; let them return <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> every man to his house in peace. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, Did I not tell thee <hi type="italic">that</hi> he would not prophesy good unto me, but evil? <hi type="super">18</hi> Again he said, Therefore hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; I saw the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and <hi type="italic">on</hi> his left. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Who shall entice Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? And one spake saying after this manner, and another saying after that manner. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then there came out a spirit, and stood before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, I will entice him. And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Wherewith? <hi type="super">21</hi> And he said, I will go out, and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And <hi type="italic">the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> </hi> said, Thou shalt entice <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and thou shalt also prevail: go out, and do <hi type="italic">even</hi> so. <hi type="super">22</hi> Now therefore, behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of these thy prophets, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken evil against thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and smote Micaiah upon the cheek, and said, Which way went the Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from me to speak unto thee? <hi type="super">24</hi> And Micaiah said, Behold, thou shalt see on that day when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then the king of Israel said, Take ye Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son; <hi type="super">26</hi> And say, Thus saith the king, Put this <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I return in peace. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Micaiah said, If thou certainly return in peace, <hi type="italic">then</hi> hath not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spoken by me. And he said, Hearken, all ye people. <div eID="gen8215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8216" type="x-p"/> This is almost word for word the same with what we had, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.41-1Kgs.22.50">1 Kings xxii.</reference> We will not repeat what was there said, nor have we much to add, but may take occasion to think, 1. Of the great duty of acknowledging God in all our ways <hi type="italic">and enquiring at his word,</hi> whatever we undertake. Jehoshaphat was not willing to proceed till he had done this, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.4">v. 4</reference>. By particular believing prayer, by an unbiased consultation of the scripture and our own consciences, and by an observant regard to the hints of providence, we may make such enquiries and very much to our satisfaction. 2. Of the great danger of bad company even to good men. Those that have more wisdom, grace, and resolution, cannot be sure that they can converse familiarly with wicked people and get no hurt by them. Jehoshaphat here, in complaisance to Ahab, sits in his robes, patiently hearing the false prophets speaking lies in the name of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.9">v. 9</reference>), can scarcely find in his heart to give him a too mild and gentle reproof for hating a prophet of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.7">v. 7</reference>), and dares not rebuke that false prophet who basely abused the faithful seer nor oppose Ahab who committed him to prison. Those who venture among the seats of the scornful cannot come off without a great deal of the guilt attaching to at least the omission of their duty, unless they have such measures of wisdom and courage as few can pretend to. 3. Of the unhappiness of those who are surrounded with flatterers, especially flattering prophets, who cry peace to them and prophesy nothing but smooth things. Thus was Ahab cheated into his ruin, and justly; for he hearkened to such, and preferred those that humoured him before a good prophet that gave him fair warning of his danger. Those do best for themselves that give their friends leave, and particularly their ministers, to deal plainly and faithfully with them, and take their reproofs not only patiently, but kindly. That counsel is not always best for us that is most pleasing to us. 4. Of the power of Satan, by the divine permission, <hi type="italic">in the children of disobedience.</hi> One lying spirit can make 400 lying prophets and make use of them to deceive Ahab, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.21">v. 21</reference>. The devil becomes a murderer by being a liar and destroys men by deceiving them. 5. Of the justice of God in giving those up to strong delusions, to believe a lie, who will not receive the love of the truth, but rebel against it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.21">v. 21</reference>. Let the <hi type="italic">lying spirit prevail</hi> to entice those to their ruin that will not be persuaded to their duty and happiness. 6. Of the hard case of faithful ministers, whose lot it has often been to be hated, and persecuted, and ill-treated, for being true to their God and just and kind to the souls of men. Micaiah, for discharging a good conscience, was buffeted, imprisoned, and condemned to the bread and water of affliction. But he could with assurance appeal to the issue, as all those may do who are persecuted for their faithfulness, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.27">v. 27</reference>. The day will declare who is in the right and who in the wrong, when Christ will appear, to the unspeakable consolation of his persecuted people and the everlasting confusion of their persecutors, who will be made <hi type="italic">to see in that day</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.24">v. 24</reference>) what they will not now believe.
entries.6adb1f9c87f2290e27bb1ae89685e2d858c364cb: <div eID="gen8216" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ahab Slain in Battle. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen8217" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. <hi type="super">29</hi> And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, I will disguise myself, and will go to the battle; but put thou on thy robes. So the king of Israel disguised himself; and they went to the battle. <hi type="super">30</hi> Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of the chariots that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, saying, Fight ye not with small or great, save only with the king of Israel. <hi type="super">31</hi> And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, It <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king of Israel. Therefore they compassed about him to fight: but Jehoshaphat cried out, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> helped him; and God moved them <hi type="italic">to depart</hi> from him. <hi type="super">32</hi> For it came to pass, that, when the captains of the chariots perceived that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back again from pursuing him. <hi type="super">33</hi> And a <hi type="italic">certain</hi> man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: therefore he said to his chariot man, Turn thine hand, that thou mayest carry me out of the host; for I am wounded. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the battle increased that day: howbeit the king of Israel stayed <hi type="italic">himself</hi> up in <hi type="italic">his</hi> chariot against the Syrians until the even: and about the time of the sun going down he died. <div eID="gen8217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8218" type="x-p"/> We have here, 1. Good Jehoshaphat exposing himself in his robes, thereby endangered, and yet delivered. We have reason to think that Ahab, while he pretended friendship, really aimed at Jehoshaphat's life, to take him off, that he might have the management of his successor, who was his son-in-law, else he would never have advised him to enter into the battle with his robes on, which was but to make himself an easy mark to the enemy: and, if really he intended that, it was as unprincipled a piece of treachery as ever man was guilty of, and justly was he himself taken in the pit he digged for his friend. The enemy had soon an eye upon the robes, and vigorously attacked the unwary prince who now, when it was too late, wished himself in the habit of the poorest soldier, rather than in his princely raiment. He cried out, either to his friends to relieve him (but Ahab took no care of that), or to his enemies, to rectify their mistake, and let them know that he was not the king of Israel. Or perhaps he cried to God for succour and deliverance (to whom else should he cry?) and he found it was not in vain: <hi type="italic">The Lord helped him out</hi> of his distress, by <hi type="italic">moving the captains to depart from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.31">v. 31</reference>. God has all men's hearts in his hand, and turns them as he pleases, contrary to their own first intentions, to serve his purposes. Many are moved unaccountably both to themselves and others, but an invisible power moves them. 2. Wicked Ahab disguising himself, arming himself thereby as he thought securing himself, and yet slain, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.33">v. 33</reference>. No art, no arms, can save those whom God has appointed to ruin. What can hurt those whom God will protect? And what can shelter those whom God will destroy? Jehoshaphat is safe in his robes, Ahab killed in his armour; for the race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong.  <chapter eID="2Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen8218" type="x-p"/>

entries.a41d652262d01cb7592227e8f6dbe79d9b573d50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4039"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <div sID="gen5849" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1-2Chr.18.34">2Ch 18:1-34</reference>. Jehoshaphat and Ahab Go against Ramoth-gilead.<div eID="gen5849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4039"/><hi type="bold">2. after certain years he went down to Ahab to Samaria--</hi>This is word for word, the same as <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.53">1Ki 22:1-53</reference>. (See commentary on that chapter). <chapter eID="2Chr.18"/>

entries.8e58272224d74152eba5aab7ccb50cfd13564671: <div eID="gen14323" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14324" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14324" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14326" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat joins affinity with Ahab, king of Israel, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Chr 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2">2Chr 18:2</reference>; who invites him to assist him in the war against the Syrians, to which Jehoshaphat agrees, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.3">2Chr 18:3</reference>. They consult the prophets concerning the success of the war; and all, except Micaiah, promise Ahab victory, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.4-2Chr.18.17">2Chr 18:4-17</reference>. Micaiah relates his vision concerning the lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab's prophets, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.18-2Chr.18.22">2Chr 18:18-22</reference>. Zedekiah, a false prophet, opposes Micaiah; and Micaiah is put in prison, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.23-2Chr.18.27">2Chr 18:23-27</reference>. Both the kings go against the Syrians; the confederate armies are defeated, and the king of Israel slain, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.28-2Chr.18.31">2Chr 18:28-31</reference>. <div eID="gen14326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14327" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14328" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat had riches and honor - The preceding chapter gives ample proof of this. <div eID="gen14328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14329" type="x-p"/> Joined affinity with Ahab - Took his daughter Athalia to be wife to his son Joram.
entries.05be9eb89aa3398cf6ed2403d00dcbd79b254339: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14330" type="x-p"/> To Ramoth-gilead - This place belonged to the Israelites, and was now held by the king of Syria. <div eID="gen14330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14331" type="x-p"/> The whole of this chapter is circumstantially explained in the notes on 1 Kings 22:1-53.
entries.1ed3961cb11300010696cfc5c987c4870f112208: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14332" type="x-p"/> The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat - "Ahab consulted false prophets; but Jehoshaphat sought instruction from the presence of the Lord, and prayed at the entering in of Samaria; and before these all the false prophets prophesied lies." - Targum.
entries.a3e3513f1a9459ac4dfc89c757afeea89c39f54e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen14332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14333" type="x-p"/> Then there came out a spirit - The Targum gives a strange gloss here: "Then the spirit of Naboth of Jezreel came out from the abode of the righteous, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will deceive him. And the Lord said, By what means? To which he answered, I will be a spirit of false prophecy in the mouth of his prophets. And the Lord said, Thou mayest then. But although the power of deceiving them is given unto thee, nevertheless it will not be lawful for thee to sit among the righteous; for whosoever shall speak falsely cannot have a mansion among the righteous. Therefore go forth from me, and do as thou hast said." - Targum.
entries.2fece435928c970368ccdbae176586f0ca76925a: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen14333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14334" type="x-p"/> I will disguise myself - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.30">1Kgs 22:30</reference>.
entries.da2c0f884d7c767d9c384e07ab60cc821b6a3a32: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen14334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14335" type="x-p"/> But Jehoshaphat cried out - "Jehoshaphat cried, and the Word of the Lord brought him assistance." - Targum.
entries.1ee2bcfbcf64f41a26b73f219587471c98db2fe1: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen14335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14336" type="x-p"/> A certain man drew a bow - The Targum tells us who it was. "Now, Naaman, the captain of the host of the great king of Syria, drew a bow against him, (that the prophecy of Elijah the Tishbite, and of Micaiah the son of Imla, might be fulfilled), and smote the king of Israel between the heart and the caul of the liver, through the place where the coat of mail is joined." See the note on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.1">2Kgs 5:1</reference> for this tradition.
entries.c070184ebd66c1f157b7b58ee6f83b2c8a363ac1: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen14336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14337" type="x-p"/> Stayed himself up - against the Syrians - There was a great deal of true personal courage and patriotism in this last act of the king of Israel: he well knew that if his troops found that he was mortally wounded, they would immediately give way, and the battle would not only be lost, but the slaughter would be great in the pursuit; therefore he stayed himself up till the evening, when the termination of the day must necessarily bring the battle to a close: and when this was done, the Israelites found that their king was slain, and so they left the field of battle to their foes. Thus Israel had a great loss, and the Syrians had got a great deliverance. Had it not been for this accident, the Syrians had probably been defeated. See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.36">1Kgs 22:36</reference> (note). <div eID="gen14337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14338" type="x-p"/> In the notes referred to above, the quibbling predictions of false prophets and lying oracles are mentioned, and several instances given; and the whole account of the lying spirit going forth from the Lord to deceive Ahab, particularly considered. See especially the notes as above on <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.19">2Chr 18:19</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.23-2Chr.18.24">2Chr 18:23-24</reference> (note). <div eID="gen14338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14339" type="x-p"/> The reader should never forget a truth so very frequently occurring in the Bible, that God is repeatedly represented as doing what, in the course of his providence, he only permits to be done.  <chapter eID="2Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen14339" type="x-p"/>

entries.ea366bb6e7bd9f3f14063291c5f1373e6d07b09b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Ch 18:1</reference> <hi type="italic">Jehoshaphat’s marriage alliance with Ahab, and his campaign with Ahab against the Syrians at Ramoth in Gilead</hi>. - 2Ch 18:1. Jehoshaphat came into connection by marriage with Ahab through his son Joram taking Athaliah, a daughter of Ahab, to wife (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.6">2Ch 21:6</reference>); an event which did not take place on the visit made by Jehoshaphat to Ahab in his palace at Samaria, and recorded in <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2">2Ch 18:2</reference>, but which had preceded that by about nine years. That visit falls in the beginning of the year in which Ahab was mortally wounded at Ramoth, and died, i.e., the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat’s reign. But at that time Ahaziah, the son of Joram and Athaliah, was already from eight to nine years old, since thirteen years later he became king at the age of twenty-two; 2Ki 8:26, cf. with the chronol. table to 1 Kings 12. The marriage connection is mentioned in order to account for Jehoshaphat’s visit to Samaria (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2">2Ch 18:2</reference>), and his alliance with Ahab in the war against the Syrians; but it is also introduced by a reference to Jehoshaphat’s riches and his royal splendour, repeated from 2Ch 17:5. In the opinion of many commentators, this is stated to account for Ahab’s willingness to connect his family by marriage with that of Jehoshaphat. This opinion might be tenable were it Ahab’s entering upon a marriage connection with Jehoshaphat which is spoken of; but for Jehoshaphat, of whom it is related that he entered into a marriage connection with Ahab, his own great wealth could not be a motive for his action in that matter. If we consider, first, that this marriage connection was very hurtful to the kingdom of Judah and the royal house of David, since Athaliah not only introduced the Phoenician idolatry into the kingdom, but also at the death of Ahaziah extirpated all the royal seed of the house of David, only the infant Joash of all the royal children being saved by the princess, a sister of Ahaziah, who was married to the high priest Jehoiada (<reference osisRef="2Chr.22.10-2Chr.22.12">2Ch 22:10-12</reference>); and, second, that Jehoshaphat was sharply censured by the prophet for his alliance with the criminal Ahab (2Ch 19:2.), and had, moreover, all but forfeited his life in the war (2Ch 18:34.), - we see that the author of the Chronicle can only have regarded the marriage connection between Jehoshaphat and Ahab as a mistake. By introducing this account of it by a second reference to Jehoshaphat’s riches and power, he must therefore have intended to hint that Jehoshaphat had no need to enter into this relationship with the idolatrous house of Ahab, but had acted very inconsiderately in doing so. Schmidt has correctly stated the contents of the verse thus: <hi type="italic">Josaphatus cetera dives et gloriosus infelicem adfinitatem cum Achabo, rege Israelis, contrahit</hi>. With which side the proposals for thus connecting the two royal houses originated we are not anywhere informed. Even if the conjecture of Ramb., that Ahab proposed it to Jehoshaphat, be not well founded, yet so much is beyond doubt, namely, that Ahab not only desired the alliance, but also promoted it by every means in his power, since it must have been of great importance to him to gain in Jehoshaphat a strong ally against the hostile pressure of the Syrians. Jehoshaphat probably entered upon the alliance <hi type="italic">bono animo et spe firmandae inter duo regna pacis</hi> (Ramb.), without much thought of the dangers which a connection of this sort with the idolatrous Ahab and with Jezebel might bring upon his kingdom.
entries.1f880ae8a7975b7153e87ed62368c96ad0107e80: <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2-2Chr.18.34">2Ch 18:2-34</reference> <hi type="italic">The campaign undertaken along with Ahab against the Syrians</hi> at Ramoth in Gilead, with its origin, course, and results for Ahab, is narrated in 1 Kings (in the history of Ahab) in agreement with our narrative, only the introduction to the war being different here. In 1Ki 22:1-3 it is remarked, in connection with the preceding wars of Ahab with the Syrians, that after there had been no war for three years between Aram and Israel, in the third year Jehoshaphat king of Judah came up to the king of Israel; and the latter, when he and his servants had determined to snatch away from the Syrians the city Ramoth in Gilead, which belonged to Israel, called upon Jehoshaphat to march with him to the war against Ramoth. In the Chronicle the more exact statement, “in the third year,” which is intelligible only in connection with the earlier history of Ahab, is exchanged for the indefinite שׁנים לקץ, “at the end of years;” and mention is made of the festal entertainment which Ahab bestowed upon his guest and his train (עמּו אשׁר העם), to show the pains which Ahab took to induce King Jehoshaphat to take part in the proposed campaign. He killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, ויסיתהוּ ,ecnadn, and enticed, seduced him to go up with him to Ramoth. הסית, to incite, entice to anything (Jdg 1:14), frequently to evil; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.13.7">Deu 13:7</reference>, etc. עלה, to advance upon a land or a city in a warlike sense. The account which follows of the preparations for the campaign by inquiring of prophets, and of the war itself, vv. 4-34, is in almost verbal agreement with 1 Kings 22:5-35. Referring to 1 Kings for the commentary on the substance of the narrative, we will here only group together briefly the divergences. Instead of 400 men who were prophets, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.5">2Ch 18:5</reference>, in 1Ki 22:5 we have about 400 men. It is a statement in round numbers, founded not upon exact enumeration, but upon an approximate estimate. Instead of אהדּל אם...הנלך, <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.5">2Ch 18:5</reference>, in Kings, 1Ki 22:6, we have אהדּל אם...האלך, both verbs being in the same number; and so too in <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.14">2Ch 18:14</reference>, where in Kings. 1Ki 22:15, both verbs stand in the plural, notwithstanding that the answer which follows, והצלח עלה, is addressed to Ahab alone, not to both the kings, while in the Chronicle the answer is given in the plural to both the kings, והצליחוּ עלוּ. in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Chr.18.7">2Ch 18:7</reference></hi>, “he prophesies me nothing good, but all his days (i.e., so long as he has been a prophet) evil,” the meaning is intensified by the כּל־ימיו, which is not found in 1Ki 22:8. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.9">2Ch 18:9</reference>, the ויושׁבים, which is introduced before the בּגרן, “and sitting upon the threshing-floor,” is due to difference of style, for it is quite superfluous for the signification. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.15">2Ch 18:15</reference>, the ambiguous words of Micah,' and Jahve will give into the hand of the king” (1Ki 22:15), are given in a more definite form: “and they (the enemy) shall be given into your hand.” In <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.19">2Ch 18:19</reference>, in the first כּכה אמר זה, the אמר after the preceding ויּאמר is not only superfluous, but improper, and has probably come into the text by a copyist’s error. We should therefore read only בּכה זה, corresponding to the כּכה זה of 1Ki 22:20 : “Then spake one after this manner, and the other spake after another manner.” In <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.23">2Ch 18:23</reference>, the indefinite אי־זה of 1Ki 22:24, is elucidated by הדּרך זה אי, “is that the manner” (cf. 1Ki 13:12; 2Ki 3:8)., and the <hi type="italic">verb</hi>. עבר follows without the relative pronoun, as in the passages cited. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.30">2Ch 18:30</reference>, only הרכב שׂרי of the king are mentioned, without any statement of the number, which is given in 1Ki 22:31, with a backward reference to the former war (1Ki 20:24). In <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.31">2Ch 18:31</reference>, after the words, “and Jehoshaphat cried out,” the higher cause of Jehoshaphat’s rescue is pointed out in the words, “and Jahve helped him, and God drove them from him,” which are not found in 1Ki 22:32; but by this religious reflection the actual course of the event is in no way altered. Bertheau’s remark, therefore, that “the words disturb the clear connection of the events,” is quite unwarrantable. Finally, in <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.34">2Ch 18:34</reference>, מעמיד היה, he was holding his position, i.e., he held himself standing upright, the Hiph. is more expressive than the Hoph. מעמד (1Ki 22:35), since it expresses more definitely the fact that he held himself upright by his own strength. With Ahab’s death, which took place in the evening at the time of the going down of the sun, the author of the Chronicle concludes his account of this war, and proceeds in <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.1-2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:1-11</reference> to narrate the further course of Jehoshaphat’s reign. In 1Ki 22:36-39, the return of the defeated army, and the details as to Ahab’s death and burial, are recorded; but these did not fit into the plan of the Chronicle.  <chapter eID="2Chr.18"/> <div eID="gen6044" type="x-p"/>
